channel.title: Paweł Jankiewicz
channel.description: Blog about programming, AI, Machine Learning

item.title: Your release build has never run
item.description: Debug builds run a thousand times before shipping. The release build often runs zero times. That asymmetry is where launch bugs hide.

item.title: Your guardrails will lose arguments to a smarter model
item.description: I upgraded an AI product to a stronger model and my hallucination guard started losing debates to it — in front of users. What "smarter" breaks, and how to fix the referee instead of the player.

item.title: Your agent isn't dumb, your simulator is rigged
item.description: I spent hours tuning a game bot that kept dying at level one. The bot was fine. The world it lived in was broken in ways that looked exactly like bad play.

item.title: The judge must see everything the model saw
item.description: My eval pipeline filed four hallucination defects in three days. All four were false accusations — the judge was blind to one input stream.

item.title: The stall wasn't in my code — the GPU process was collecting my garbage
item.description: A WebGPU animation froze for half a second every few seconds. The profiler said my code was innocent. The real culprit was 4.5 GB/s of texture allocations nobody could see.

item.title: The bug was in the path nobody ran
item.description: A feature can pass every test and still be broken — if your tests take a different road through it than production does.

item.title: Capabilities you can't call beat capabilities you're told not to use
item.description: Sandboxing user scripts? Don't gate the dangerous functions with flags. Build a second environment where they don't exist.

item.title: Silence is not a green light
item.description: My build gate reported a perfect batch — 195 files, zero failures. 190 of them had never been compiled at all. The lesson: never let a pipeline count the absence of errors as success.

item.title: Other People's Codebases Are the Best Test Suite You Never Wrote
item.description: When you build a tool that rewrites source code, the strongest test isn't your fixtures — it's running it on real third-party projects and checking they still compile and pass their own tests.

item.title: The click that never happened
item.description: I spent an hour debugging an app bug that didn't exist. The test harness was silently throwing my clicks into the void.

item.title: Every URL returned 200
item.description: A server that answers OK to a page that does not exist, and four other bugs that were invisible because success and silence look identical.

item.title: Code Behind a Feature Flag Has Never Been Compiled
item.description: A screenshot function sat in a vendored framework looking finished. The first time any build actually enabled its feature, it failed twice — once at compile time, once at runtime. Dead code at least type-checks. Feature-gated code doesn't even do that.

item.title: My Backtracker Counted the Same Answer 5,040 Times
item.description: A backtracking search kept reporting 'ambiguous' on inputs with exactly one solution. The search was correct — it was just enumerating every solution in every possible order, and tripping its own safety cap.

item.title: A screenshot is not a click
item.description: Static screenshots of a web app will happily show you a beautiful, broken feature. Driving the app found a bug in ten minutes that a hundred passing tests missed — with a CDP driver in 100 lines and zero dependencies.

item.title: The Least-Tested State Is the Most Common One
item.description: A conversion widget shipped invisible because every test ran as a returning user. The fresh visitor — cookie banner up, nothing decided — is the state nobody tests and everybody lives in.

item.title: Your oracle has bugs too
item.description: Differential testing against a reference implementation works great — until the reference is wrong. What a red CI on exactly one OS taught me about oracle tests.

item.title: The Tree Was Correct and Still Wrong
item.description: A scene tree built faithfully from a data-flow graph confused everyone who looked at it. The data was right. The orientation was backwards.

item.title: Your monolith is probably already a DAG
item.description: We assume big crates are too tangled to split. Most of the time the tangle is imaginary — and measurable.

item.title: Retrying Is Not Replanning
item.description: Why AI code generation needs to redo the plan, not just redo the function

item.title: UX testing is the bottleneck — Playwright MCP closes the loop
item.description: Backend is solid. Frontend is fine. UX testing eats the rest of your day.

item.title: Arnimate: A 2D Animation Editor Built in Rust
item.description: Announcing Arnimate, a 2D vector animation editor built with Rust, wgpu, and egui. Think Adobe Animate, but native, GPU-accelerated, and free to use in your browser via WebAssembly.

item.title: egui-shadcn: Beautiful UI Components for Rust
item.description: Announcing egui-shadcn, a library that brings shadcn/ui-style components to egui — 55+ widgets with built-in theming, from buttons and inputs to dialogs and date pickers.

item.title: To Err is AI
item.description: Why 80% AI performance is still good

item.title: Zen Coding: Building Software That AI Can Understand and Evolve
item.description: How to write software with AI

item.title: Rust is the most important language at the moment
item.description: Why I think Rust is and will become the most important language for AI-assisted software development

item.title: My Take: The Frameworkless Future with AI
item.description: Why I think AI might just kill our reliance on dodgy open-source libraries by cooking up code on the fly.
